previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of type 1 diabetes, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, chronic systolic heart failure, seizure disorder, and esophageal reflux was admitted from transplant clinic with a one-day history of fever, myalgias, dizziness, and diarrhea. Initial evaluation revealed a low-grade fever and stable vital signs after IV fluids. Chest X-ray showed clear lungs and no free air, and EKG was unchanged. Rapid flu testing was negative, and blood cultures showed no growth. His symptoms were attributed to a mild viral upper respiratory infection. He received supportive care, including hydration and antipyretics, and completed his scheduled hemodialysis. He improved rapidly, afebrile by the morning of discharge, and was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to continue his home medications and follow up with his specialists.

# Dialysis graft bleed: The patient's dialysis graft appeared 
non-infected on admission and was structurally intact. 
B-mode/Doppler ultrasound was unremarkable save a small focal 
hematoma. Later on the day of acceptance he was noted to have 
serosanguinous oozing. Transplant surgery re-evaluated the graft 
and it appeared that this was related to repeated needle stick 
at the same site. This stabilized over the next ___ hours and 
did not ooze for at least the last 24 hours he spent in 
hospital.
.
# Colitis: This was noted on abdominal CT at time of admission. 
Of note, CT was done given history of abdominal pain mentioned 
in HPI, but patient was pain free by time of initial interview 
and as described in exam, without physical findings. Question 
infectious vs cytokine-mediated in setting of sepsis. Notably, 
the patient had no diarrhea or abdominal pain, except following 
Miralax several days into hospitalization.

no accompanying diarrhea and although colitis noted on CT as 
mentioned above, no correlate on exam. He did have nbnb emesis 
(gastric contents) early in his hospital course. This was 
markedly improved post dialysis and he tolerated PO very well 
from the time of his first dialysis session until discharge.

# Hypoxia: The patient sustained a transient desat in ED. 
Subsequently, he satured well on RA and breathed comfortably for 
the remainder of his hospital course. CXR was consistent with 
mild pulmonary edema but this was not clinically significant. He 
was neither short of breath nor hypoxic while on the medicine 
service.
